title: Report on Studying at Duke University and McGill University
paragraphs: I did one-month clerkships each at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, and McGill University in Montreal. Both are universities known worldwide in fields other than medicine as well, and I feel very honored to have been given such a valuable opportunity. In this report I will divide the discussion into five major sections: "Clerkship at Duke University," "Life in Durham," "Clerkship at McGill University," "Life in Montreal," and "What I learned through the clerkships as a whole." In order to describe my experience as it was, as far as possible, the text may lose some coherence, and I ask for your understanding.

At Duke it was the Hematology-Oncology program, and I spent one month in the outpatient clinics of Oncology and Hematology. Before describing the content of the clerkship, let me first explain how oncology is organised in the United States.

In the United States, all cancer patients are seen by the Oncology Department. Of course it handles not only the treatment of outpatients but also the management of inpatients. The Oncology Department is divided by organ or disease into Divisions such as Pulmonary Oncology and Malignant Hematology, and each doctor treats the tumors of their own specialty. In Japan, departments are first divided by organ, and each department sees both malignant and benign diseases, but in the United States, benign and malignant diseases are first sharply separated and then divided into the respective specialties. I think it is the same in other large hospitals, but at Duke there is a facility dedicated to oncology alone, the Duke Cancer Center, attached to the clinic and the ward, and all outpatient consultations and treatment were done here.

As for the content of the clerkship, I basically went to the clinic designated for each day of the week (Monday: GYN, Tuesday: GI, Wednesday and Thursday: Malignant Hematology, Friday: Benign Hematology) and examined several patients assigned from the attending's (or resident's) schedule. Specifically, I obtained information on the assigned patients in advance from the electronic medical record and from faxes sent from other hospitals, went to the examination room, took the history and did the physical examination, then presented to the attending and accompanied the attending on the main examination. (As a side note, in the United States a single doctor is in charge of several examination rooms; the patient is led to a room first and the doctor comes in afterward to examine.) After the main examination I also wrote the chart note. It was exactly the H&P that I had practised many times in the pre-departure training, and I felt really glad that I had trained for it. Most of the attending's schedule consisted of return patients, so naturally I had many opportunities to see return patients, but I was often assigned new patients too, and then I desperately read through the dozens of pages of faxed material to do the examination. The attendings looked busy but were all friendly, and after the presentation and after the main examination I received feedback on the disease and the patient's background, so I felt I was learning from my own experience. It was a little disappointing that there were no other students in the same rotation and that I had no involvement in ward work, but by seeing many patients in the outpatient clinic I could learn while getting a picture of how cancer patients' symptoms and side effects present, and of the flow of treatment and follow-up, so I felt it was very meaningful. On days when the attending was absent I also visited other clinics, and as one example I was given the chance, only once, to do a clerkship in a sickle cell disease clinic. It is a disease rarely seen in Japan, and a specialty clinic for it is unthinkable in Japan, so it was a truly valuable experience.
The clerkship at Duke was full of surprises, and among them there were three that surprised me especially.

The first is the existence of the Physician Assistant (PA). If you look up "physician assistant" in the Merriam-Webster dictionary, it says "a person certified to provide basic medical services usually under the supervision of a licensed physician." Judging from the definition, the work of PAs is varied, so I cannot say what role PAs play at other hospitals, but at least at the Duke Cancer Center, each attending had one PA, who not only managed the day's schedule and did administrative work but also did pre-visit history-taking and even simple follow-up. I got a glimpse of the effort to make medical care run smoothly and efficiently by actively dividing labor and increasing the number of comedical staff.

The second is that clinical trials are conducted very actively. If you walk along the clinic corridors, you notice posters calling for participation in clinical trials everywhere. What is even more surprising is that there is a profession dedicated to clinical trials, with offices on each floor. These people specialised in managing the enrollment and requirements of each trial and in obtaining and managing evaluation data. For doctors alone, while doing their regular clinical work, to remember the contents, indications and exclusion criteria of different trials, to assess disease status more frequently than in regular treatment, and at the same time to fill in and manage complicated and numerous documents would be quite hard work. So I realised that by again making good use of the division of labor, the many clinical trials can be advanced without losing momentum.

The third is the American insurance system. In the United States there is some public insurance, such as Medicaid for low-income people and Medicare for the elderly, but ordinary people basically join private insurance companies. Moreover, insurance companies and insurance plans differ by state, so the care one can receive depends greatly on the coverage and out-of-pocket amount of one's insurance plan. This is about the GI Oncology clinic I attended every Tuesday: the attending I was with saw many patients with neuroendocrine tumors (NET). As a new treatment for NET from the third line onward, there is Lutathera®, a somatostatin analog bound to a radioactive substance, which received FDA approval on January 29, 2018. However, in April 2018, when I was doing my clerkship, none of the insurance companies in North Carolina had come to a conclusion on whether to cover the treatment cost, so the reality was that no one could receive treatment unless they paid the whole high treatment cost out of pocket. I saw many patients who could not receive treatment and went home disappointed. Some even relied on the Duke Cancer Center and traveled all the way from the suburbs, more than five hours one way, to seek a second opinion. Just because it has been approved by the nation does not mean it can actually be used in treatment. For patients who place hope in a new treatment, it was a rather cruel reality. Regarding Lutathera®, I sincerely hope that each insurance company will announce its position as soon as possible.

This year again I visited the home of Jenny and Fred, my host family who have looked after me every year, and fully enjoyed the American lifestyle. Although they are in different laboratories, both of them work in a microbiology laboratory at Duke. Both were affable and kind, and I spent enjoyable days: we went to eat Southern specialties such as pork BBQ and pecan pie, they invited me to their favorite Italian restaurant that uses local ingredients, and we made decorated eggs together to celebrate Easter. They also took me to a park along the Eno River in the suburbs, where they volunteer on weekends to maintain the walking trails, and I walked their dog Birdie.

Durham is a university town that exists because of Duke University. I arbitrarily think that the "D" in "Durham" is the "D" in "Duke". The town is calm and green, and even off campus, on the streets and in cafes, I saw many students and university people wearing hoodies and T-shirts with the "DUKE" logo. In the university library and in cafes in town, I was stimulated every day by the "Blue Devils" working hard on their assignments with MacBooks plastered with Duke stickers. It would be sacrilege to ask for a better environment for studying.

At McGill too I did a one-month clerkship in the Oncology outpatient clinic. Incidentally, McGill University is also famous as the university where EBM originated. The place I went to was the Jewish General Hospital (JGH), the second teaching hospital. It is located in a relatively central part of the city, about five or six subway stations from downtown. Montreal, where McGill is located, is in French-speaking Quebec, but perhaps because McGill is a university with English-language roots, conversations among doctors and conferences were in English. Patients are also almost all bilingual, so I had almost no trouble communicating in English. If you go to the neighboring province of Ontario, where Toronto is, everything is in English, so it is natural to be bilingual.

To be frank, as far as the oncology system is concerned, I felt there was no particular difference between the United States and Canada. JGH too has a clinic and outpatient treatment facility specialising in oncology called the Segal Cancer Centre, which exists separately from the general clinics that see benign diseases. As far as I experienced, I also felt there was not much difference between the United States and Canada in treatment methods or in the activity of clinical trials. During the clerkship I had a chance to talk with a resident who had graduated from a US medical school, done two years of residency there, and then returned to his hometown of Montreal, and he also said that at least in the field of oncology there is not much difference between the United States and Canada (Quebec). If there is a difference, he said, the United States is better in the speed to treatment. However, although it surely depends on the size and staff of the hospital, I felt that JGH had a stronger General Oncology character than the Duke Cancer Center. This is because at the Segal Cancer Centre many doctors belong to multiple Divisions and run outpatient clinics for different cancer types depending on the day of the week. For example, one of the attendings who looked after me ran breast cancer and GI clinics on Mondays and Fridays and saw lung cancer on Wednesdays. It is a sight that can hardly be seen in Japan at least, so it was shocking to me. I remember that this doctor asked me with a puzzled look, "In Japan, pulmonologists treat lung cancer?" I realised anew that there are great differences in the systems of cancer care between Japan and Canada (and the United States).

The content of the clerkship was basically the same as at Duke: every week I went to the attending who had an outpatient clinic on a given day of the week, and took histories and did physical examinations of assigned patients, presented, and wrote chart notes. Here too I had the opportunity to examine patients with various cancer types, such as breast cancer, GI cancer, lung cancer, GU cancer and melanoma, and I learned a great deal.

From what I have written so far you might think that there is no difference between American and Canadian healthcare, but that is by no means the case. Probably the biggest difference is the insurance system. Medical care in Canada is free and covered entirely by taxes. However, the cost of therapeutic drugs is out of pocket, so ordinary people buy insurance to reduce the out-of-pocket amount. When I first went to JGH, I was impressed that patients who had finished their consultation all just made appointments for their next visit or tests at the reception and left the hospital as they were. However, this free medical care does not seem to be all good: because the threshold for patients to seek care is low, "waiting" at medical institutions has become a problem. This problem seems especially evident in emergency departments, and one patient I saw after colon cancer surgery told me with an exasperated look that when he previously visited the emergency department for lower back pain he was made to wait for more than 12 hours. I think it was fortunate at least that bone metastasis was ruled out, though.

Montreal is called "the Paris of North America," and the city is clean and open-terrace cafes can be seen everywhere. The old town in the downtown area in particular is full of charm, with horse-drawn carriages going back and forth on the cobblestones and the sound of a street performer's saxophone coming from somewhere. Notre-Dame Basilica, at the heart of the old town, is famous for its magnificent decoration based on blue, reminiscent of Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, and is worth a visit.

In Montreal I stayed through the private-lodging site Airbnb near a subway station about a five-minute walk from the hospital. In the same house there were three other students on long stays like me: a German girl who was also doing a hospital clerkship at McGill, an Italian boy enrolled in a doctoral course in the engineering faculty of the University of Montreal, and a French girl majoring in physics, also at the University of Montreal. Every evening at dinnertime we would gather one after another in the dining room and spend a pleasant time talking about our home countries while eating. Germany, Italy, France, Japan. From the outside it looks like some international conference. Shall we call ourselves the G4?
In this last section, I would like to take up two major things I learned through the total of two months of clerkships in the United States and Canada.

The first is that the polyclinic clerkship in Japan is not the whole of medical education. In both the United States and Canada, I felt they place great importance on "exposure." Rather than just showing students the clinical setting and leaving them as outsiders, they place students in the clinical setting and have them think for themselves, pushing them to the point of how to assess the patient's current condition and, following that assessment, what the treatment will be, and I felt that through this the thinking process in real clinical practice and the actual management of patients become part of the student. This method also has the advantage that, because the required level is high, what I can and cannot do becomes clear and the challenges I should overcome in the future become visible. I learned the importance of generating learning from my own experience.

The second is the true meaning of EBM. To be honest, until this study abroad I thought that EBM meant strictly carrying out the standard treatment in accordance with guidelines. In reality, however, from the results of clinical trials reported every day, I learned that when patients are divided into subsets by patient characteristics and prognostic factors, the current standard treatment does not necessarily bring the best outcome for that patient. (Of course, later on, standard treatments that take such factors into account will be reflected in guidelines one after another, and the guidelines will become more complex and thicker.) While in McGill's Oncology, I attended the Tumor Board held every week, and I vividly remember the doctors actively discussing the treatment plans for the cases under review while citing papers. From this I learned that EBM means correctly interpreting the evidence produced every day and providing the treatment thought to be optimal at present while matching it against the patient's characteristics and wishes.

Finally, I would like to offer my greatest thanks to Dr. 長谷川 and Dr. 粕谷 and the staff of the International Collaboration Office, who supported this valuable experience of studying abroad, to the professors of Duke and McGill who hosted me, to my host family Jenny and Fred, and to my parents. Thank you very much.
